entry.description: The child reads a word that names a relationship between two things (contrast, unless, however, instead of) as its opposite, usually as plain 'and' or 'the same as'. The result is an option that keeps every fact but reverses how the facts sit together.
entry.childHint: Some words tell you how two things go together. Find that word and read it again.

stem.text: Read lines 36 to 41. The writer suddenly says: 'What a contrast between him and his friend!' Why is that sentence put there?

carriers.key: To make the reader notice how differently the two men were behaving.

options.value: To tell the reader that the two men had fallen out.
To show that Mr Bingley was cross about something.
To show that the writer likes Mr Darcy the better of the two.
To make the reader notice how differently the two men were behaving.
To show that the two men were really rather alike.
options.execution: 'Contrast' is read as its opposite. The sentence says the two men are unlike, and this answers that they are alike.

options.execution: Drops the 'if' in line 53; lines 57 and 58 say she expected him to come in the morning.

options.value: She can turn a hard situation into something lovely.
She is never frightened by anything at all.
She has slept outdoors many times before.

options.value: A great deal of noisy fuss.
